entries.4066c907d45f1bf9996a3a4fdbddd464b5b9908a: <div sID="gen12229" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="97" osisID="Ps.97" sID="Ps.97"/> <div eID="gen12229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12230" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12231" type="x-p"/> This psalm dwells upon the same subject, and is set to the same tune, with the foregoing psalm. Christ is the Alpha and the Omega of both; they are both penned, and are both to be sung to his honour; and we make nothing of them if we do not, in them, make melody with our hearts to the Lord Jesus. He it is that reigns, to the joy of all mankind (<reference osisRef="Ps.97.1">ver. 1</reference>); and his government speaks, I. Terror to his enemies; for he is a prince of inflexible justice and irresistible power, <reference osisRef="Ps.97 Ps.2">ver. 2-7</reference>. II. Comfort to his friends and loyal subjects, arising from his sovereign dominion, the care he takes of his people, and the provision he makes for them, <reference osisRef="Ps.97.8-Ps.97.12">ver. 8-12</reference>. In singing this psalm we must be affected with the glory of the exalted Redeemer, must dread the lot of his enemies, and think ourselves happy if we are of those that "kiss the son."
entries.38dcace6355a651138ab88079828f92691338efc: <div eID="gen12231" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12230" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Righteousness and Glory of the Divine Government; Establishment of Christ's Kingdom.</title> <div sID="gen12232" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> reigneth; let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad <hi type="italic">thereof.</hi> <hi type="super">2</hi> Clouds and darkness <hi type="italic">are</hi> round about him: righteousness and judgment <hi type="italic">are</hi> the habitation of his throne. <hi type="super">3</hi> A fire goeth before him, and burneth up his enemies round about. <hi type="super">4</hi> His lightnings enlightened the world: the earth saw, and trembled. <hi type="super">5</hi> The hills melted like wax at the presence of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , at the presence of the Lord of the whole earth. <hi type="super">6</hi> The heavens declare his righteousness, and all the people see his glory. <hi type="super">7</hi> Confounded be all they that serve graven images, that boast themselves of idols: worship him, all <hi type="italic">ye</hi> gods. <div eID="gen12232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12233" type="x-p"/> What was to be said among the heathen in the foregoing psalm (<reference osisRef="Ps.96.10">v. 10</reference>) is here said again (<reference osisRef="Ps.97.1">v. 1</reference>) and is made the subject of this psalm, and of <reference osisRef="Ps.99.1-Ps.99.9">psalm xcix</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Lord reigns;</hi> that is the great truth here laid down. The Lord Jehovah reigns, he that made the world governs it; he that gave being gives motion and power, gives law and commission, gives success and event. Every man's judgment proceeds from the Lord, from his counsel and providence, and in all affairs, both public and private, he performs the thing which he himself has appointed. The Lord Jesus reigns; the providential kingdom is twisted in with the mediatorial and the administration of both is in the hand of Christ, who therefore is both the <hi type="italic">head of the church</hi> and <hi type="italic">head over all things to the church.</hi> The kingdom of Christ is so constituted that, <div eID="gen12233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12234" type="x-p"/> I. It may be matter of joy to all; and it will be so if it be not their own fault. <hi type="italic">Let the earth rejoice,</hi> for hereby it is <hi type="italic">established</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.96.10">Ps. xcvi. 10</reference>); it is honoured and enriched, and, in part, rescued from the vanity which by sin it is made subject to. Not only let the people of Israel rejoice in him as King of the Jews, and the daughter of Zion as her King, but let all the earth rejoice in his elevation; for the kingdoms of the world shall, more or less, sooner or later, become his kingdoms: <hi type="italic">Let the multitude of isles,</hi> the many or great isles, <hi type="italic">be glad thereof.</hi> This is applicable to our country, which is a great isle, and has many belonging to it; at least, it speaks comfort in general to the Gentiles, whose countries are called <hi type="italic">the isles of the Gentiles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.10.5">Gen. x. 5</reference>. There is enough in Christ for the multitude of the isles to rejoice in; for, though many have been made happy in him, yet still there is room. All have reason to rejoice in Christ's government. 1. In the equity of it. There is an incontestable justice in all the acts of his government, both legislative and judicial. Sometimes indeed <hi type="italic">clouds and darkness are round about him;</hi> his dispensations are altogether unaccountable; <hi type="italic">his way is in the sea and his path in the great waters.</hi> We are not aware of what he designs, what he drives at; nor is it fit that we should be let into the secrets of his government. There is a depth in his counsels, which we must not pretend to fathom. But still <hi type="italic">righteousness and judgment are the habitation of his throne;</hi> a golden thread of justice runs through the whole web of his administration. In this he resides, for it is his habitation. In this he rules, for it is <hi type="italic">the habitation of his throne. His commandments are,</hi> and will be, <hi type="italic">all righteous. Righteousness and judgment are the basis of his throne</hi> (so Dr. Hammond); for <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> his <hi type="italic">throne is for ever and ever,</hi> because his <hi type="italic">sceptre is a right sceptre,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.45.6">Ps. xlv. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">The throne is established in righteousness.</hi> Even <hi type="italic">the heavens declare his righteousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.97.6">v. 6</reference>); it is as conspicuous and as illustrious as the heavens themselves. The angels of heaven will declare it, who are employed as messengers in the administration of his government and therefore know more of it than any of his creatures. His righteousness is incontestable; for who can contradict or dispute what the <hi type="italic">heavens declare?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.6">Ps. l. 6</reference>. 2. In the extent of it in the upper and lower world. (1.) All the men on earth are under his government; either he is served by them or he serves himself by them. <hi type="italic">All the people see his glory,</hi> or may see it. The glory of God, in the face of Christ, was made to shine in distant countries, among many people, more or less among all people; the gospel was preached, for aught we know, in all languages, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.5">Acts ii. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.11">11</reference>. Miracles were wrought in all nations, and so <hi type="italic">all the people saw his glory. Have they not heard?</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.10.18">Rom. x. 18</reference>. (2.) All the angels in heaven are so. Perhaps we should not have found this truth in those words (<reference osisRef="Ps.97.7">v. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">Worship him, all you gods,</hi> if we had not been directed to it by the inspired apostle, who, from the Septuagint version of those words, makes the Messiah to be introduced into the upper world at the ascension with this charge (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.6">Heb. i. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">Let all the angels of God worship him,</hi> which helps us to a key to this whole psalm, and shows us that it must be applied to the exalted Redeemer, who has gone into heaven, <hi type="italic">and is on the right hand of God,</hi> which intimates that all power is given him both in heaven and earth, <hi type="italic">angels, authorities, and powers, being made subject unto him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.22">1 Pet. iii. 22</reference>. This speaks the honour of Christ, that he has such worshippers, and the honour of all good Christians, that they have such fellow-worshippers. <div eID="gen12234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12235" type="x-p"/> II. Christ's government, though it may be matter of joy to all, will yet be matter of terror to some, and it is their own fault that it is so, <reference osisRef="Ps.97.3-Ps.97.5">v. 3-5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.97.7">7</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen12235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12236" type="x-p"/> 1. When the kingdom of Christ was to be set up in the world, after his ascension, it would meet with many enemies, and much opposition would be given to it. He that reigns, to the <hi type="italic">joy of the whole earth,</hi> yet, as he has his subjects, so he has <hi type="italic">his enemies</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.97.3">v. 3</reference>), that not only will not have him to reign over them, but would not have him to reign at all, that not only will not <hi type="italic">enter into the kingdom of heaven themselves,</hi> but do all they can to <hi type="italic">hinder those that are entering,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.23.13">Matt. xxiii. 13</reference>. This was fulfilled in the enmity of the unbelieving Jews to the gospel of Christ, and the violent persecution which in all places they stirred up against the preachers and professors of it. These enemies are here called <hi type="italic">hills</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.97.5">v. 5</reference>), for their height, and strength, and immovable obstinacy. It was the <hi type="italic">princes of this world</hi> that <hi type="italic">crucified the Lord of glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1 Cor. ii. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.2.2">Ps. ii. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen12236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12237" type="x-p"/> 2. The opposition which the Jews gave to the setting up of Christ's kingdom turned to their own ruin. Their persecuting the apostles, and <hi type="italic">forbidding them to speak to the Gentiles,</hi> filled up their sin, and brought <hi type="italic">wrath upon them to the uttermost,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.15-1Thess.2.16">1 Thess. ii. 15, 16</reference>. That wrath is here compared, (1.) To consuming fire, which <hi type="italic">goes before him, and burns up his enemies,</hi> that have made themselves like chaff and stubble, and have <hi type="italic">set the briers and thorns before him in battle,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.27.4">Isa. xxvii. 4</reference>. This fire of divine wrath will not only burn the rubbish upon the hills, but will even <hi type="italic">melt the hills</hi> themselves <hi type="italic">like wax,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.97.5">v. 5</reference>. When our God appears as a consuming fire even rocks will be wax before him. The most resolute and daring opposition will be baffled <hi type="italic">at the presence of the Lord.</hi> His very presence is enough to shame and sink it, for he is <hi type="italic">the Lord of the whole earth,</hi> by whom all the children of men are manageable and to whom they are accountable. Men hate and persecute God's people, because they think him absent, that the Lord has <hi type="italic">forsaken the earth;</hi> but, when he manifests his presence, they melt. (2.) To amazing <hi type="italic">lightnings</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.97.4">v. 4</reference>), which strike a terror upon many. The judgments God brought upon the enemies of Christ's kingdom were such as all the world took notice of with terror: <hi type="italic">The earth saw and trembled,</hi> and the ears of all that heard were made to tingle. This was fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem and the Jewish nation by the Romans, about forty years after Christ's resurrection, which, like fire, wholly destroyed that people, and, like lightning, astonished all their neighbours (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.24">Deut. xxix. 24</reference>); but the heavens declare God's righteousness in it, and all the people, to this day, see his glory, in those lasting monuments of his justice, the scattered Jews. <div eID="gen12237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12238" type="x-p"/> 3. Idolaters also would be put to confusion by the setting up of Christ's kingdom (<reference osisRef="Ps.97.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Confounded be all those who serve graven images,</hi> the Gentile world, who <hi type="italic">did service to those that by nature are no gods</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.8">Gal. iv. 8</reference>), who boasted themselves of idols as their protectors and benefactors. Did those that served idols boast of them, and shall the servants of the living God distrust him, or be ashamed of him? <hi type="italic">Let those be ashamed that serve graven images.</hi> (1.) This is a prayer for the conversion of the Gentiles, that those who have been so long serving dumb idols may be convinced of their error, ashamed of their folly, and may, by the power of Christ's gospel, be brought to serve the only living and true God, and may be as much ashamed of their idols as ever they were proud of them. See <reference osisRef="Isa.2.20-Isa.2.21">Isa. ii. 20, 21</reference>. (2.) This is a prophecy of the ruin of those that would not be reformed and reclaimed from their idolatry; they shall be confounded by the destruction of Paganism in the Roman empire, which was fulfilled about 300 years after Christ, so much to the terror of idolaters that some think it was the revolution under Constantine that made even the mighty men say to the rocks, <hi type="italic">Fall on us and hide us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.6.15-Rev.6.16">Rev. vi. 15, 16</reference>. This prayer and prophecy are still in force against antichristian idolaters, who may here read their doom: <hi type="italic">Confounded be all those that worship graven images,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.97.7">v. 7</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Jer.48.13">Jer. xlviii. 13</reference>.
entries.88063aeadab1469c3553b87ddafc1243e4a73f95: <div eID="gen12238" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Zion Rejoicing in the Reign of Christ.</title> <div sID="gen12239" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Zion heard, and was glad; and the daughters of Judah rejoiced because of thy judgments, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">9</hi> For thou, <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">art</hi> high above all the earth: thou art exalted far above all gods. <hi type="super">10</hi> Ye that love the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , hate evil: he preserveth the souls of his saints; he delivereth them out of the hand of the wicked. 11 Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart. <hi type="super">12</hi> Rejoice in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , ye righteous; and give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness. <div eID="gen12239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12240" type="x-p"/> The kingdom of the Messiah, like the pillar of cloud and fire, as it has a dark side towards the Egyptians, so it has a bright side towards the Israel of God. It is set up in spite of opposition; and then <hi type="italic">the earth saw and trembled</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.97.4">v. 4</reference>), but <hi type="italic">Zion heard and was glad,</hi> very glad, to hear of the conversion of some and of the confusion of others, that is, the conquest of all that stood it out against Christ. <hi type="italic">Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! for behold thy king comes unto thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">Zech. ix. 9</reference>. And not Zion only, where the temple was, but even <hi type="italic">the daughters of Judah, rejoiced;</hi> the common people, the inhabitants of the villages, they shall triumph in Christ's victories. The command (<reference osisRef="Ps.97.1">v. 1</reference>) is, <hi type="italic">Let the earth rejoice;</hi> but it is only the sons of Zion and the daughters of Judah that do rejoice. All should bid the kingdom of the Messiah welcome, but few do. Now here observe, <div eID="gen12240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12241" type="x-p"/> I. The reasons that are given for Zion's joy in the government of the Redeemer. The faithful servants of God may well <hi type="italic">rejoice</hi> and be <hi type="italic">glad,</hi> 1. Because God is glorified, and whatever redounds to his honour is very much his people's pleasure. They rejoice <hi type="italic">because of thy judgments, O Lord!</hi> which may take in both the judgments of his mouth and the judgments of his hand, the word of his gospel and his works wrought for the propagating of it, miracles and marvellous providences; for in these we must own, "<hi type="italic">Thou, Lord, art high above all the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.97.9">v. 9</reference>); thou hast manifested thy sovereignty in the kingdom of nature, and thy command of all its powers, and thy dominion over all nations, over all hearts; thou art <hi type="italic">exalted far above all gods</hi>"—all deputed gods, that is, princes—all counterfeit gods, that is, idols. The exaltation of Christ, and the advancement of God's glory among men thereby, are the rejoicing of all the saints. 2. Because care is taken for their safety. Those that pay allegiance to Christ as a King shall be sure of his protection. Princes are the shields of the earth; Christ is so to his subjects; they may put their trust under his shadow and rejoice in it, for (<reference osisRef="Ps.97.10">v. 10</reference>) <hi type="italic">He preserves the souls of the saints;</hi> he preserves their lives as long as he has any work for them to do, and wonderfully <hi type="italic">delivers them</hi> many a time <hi type="italic">out of the hand of the wicked,</hi> their persecutors that thirst after their blood; for <hi type="italic">precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.</hi> But something more is meant than their lives; for those that will be his disciples must be willing to lay down their lives, and not indent for the securing of them. It is the <hi type="italic">immortal soul</hi> that Christ preserves, the <hi type="italic">inward man,</hi> which may be renewed more and more when the <hi type="italic">outward man decays.</hi> He will <hi type="italic">preserve the souls of his saints</hi> from sin, from apostasy, and despair, under their greatest trials; he will <hi type="italic">deliver them out of the hands of the wicked one</hi> that <hi type="italic">seeks to devour them; he will preserve them</hi> safely <hi type="italic">to his heavenly kingdom,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.18">2 Tim. iv. 18</reference>. They have therefore reason to be glad, being thus safe. 3. Because provision is made for their comfort. Those that rejoice in Christ Jesus, and in his exaltation, have fountains of joy treasured up for them, which will be opened sooner or later (<reference osisRef="Ps.97.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Light is sown for the righteous,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">gladness for the upright in heart.</hi> The subjects of Christ's kingdom are told to expect tribulation in the world. They must suffer by its malice, and must not share in its mirth; yet let them know, to their comfort, that <hi type="italic">light is sown</hi> for them; it is designed and prepared for them. What is sown will come up again in due time; though, like a winter seedness, it may lie long under the clods, and seem to be lost and buried, yet it will return in a rich and plentiful increase. God's goodness shall be sure of a <hi type="italic">harvest</hi> in the <hi type="italic">appointed weeks. Those that sow in tears shall,</hi> without fail, <hi type="italic">reap in joy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.126.5-Ps.126.6">Ps. cxxvi. 5, 6</reference>. Christ told his disciples, at parting (<reference osisRef="John.16.20">John xvi. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">You shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy.</hi> Gladness is sure to the <hi type="italic">upright in heart,</hi> to those only that are sincere in religion. <hi type="italic">The joy of the hypocrite is but for a moment.</hi> There is no serenity without a lasting sincerity, <div eID="gen12241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12242" type="x-p"/> II. The rules that are given for Zion's joy. 1. Let it be a pure and holy joy. "You that love the Lord Jesus, that <hi type="italic">love his appearing</hi> and kingdom, that love his word and his exaltation, see that you hate evil, the evil of sin, every thing that is offensive to him and will throw you out of his favour." Note, A true love to God will show itself in a real hatred of all sin, as that abominable thing which he hates. The joy of the saints should likewise confirm their antipathy to sin and divine comforts should put their mouths out of taste for sensual pleasures. 2. Let the joy terminate in God (<reference osisRef="Ps.97.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous.</hi> Let all the streams of comfort, which flow to us in the channel of Christ's kingdom, lead us to the fountain, and oblige us to <hi type="italic">rejoice in the Lord.</hi> All the lines of joy must meet in him as in the centre. See <reference osisRef="Php.3.3">Phil. iii. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="4.4">iv. 4</reference>. 3. Let it express itself in praise and thanksgiving: <hi type="italic">Give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness.</hi> Whatever is the matter of our rejoicing ought to be the matter of our thanksgiving, and particularly the holiness of God. Those that hate sin themselves are glad that God does so, in hopes that therefore he will not suffer it to have dominion over them. Note, (1.) We ought to be much in the remembrance of God's holiness, the infinite purity, rectitude, and perfection of the divine nature. We must be ever mindful of his holy covenant, which he has confirmed with an oath <hi type="italic">by his holiness.</hi> (2.) We ought to give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness, not only give him the glory of it as it is an honour to him, but give him thanks for it as it is a favour to us; and an unspeakable favour it will be if, through grace, we are <hi type="italic">partakers of his holiness.</hi> It is God's holiness which, above all his attributes, the angels celebrate. <reference osisRef="Isa.6.3">Isa. vi. 3</reference>, <hi type="italic">Holy, holy, holy.</hi> Sinners tremble, but saints rejoice, <hi type="italic">at the remembrance of God's holiness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.30.4">Ps. xxx. 4</reference>.  <chapter eID="Ps.97"/> <div eID="gen12242" type="x-p"/>

entries.22ca71292453590dffc3574c850a07fb3c84fdfa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6625"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 97</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.97.1-Ps.97.12">Psa 97:1-12</reference>. The writer celebrates the Lord's dominion over nations and nature, describes its effect on foes and friends, and exhorts and encourages the latter.</title> <div sID="gen10145" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6625"/>1-2. This dominion is a cause of joy, because, even though our minds are oppressed with terror before the throne of the King of kings (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.16">Ex 19:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.5.22">De 5:22</reference>), we know it is based on righteous principles and judgments which are according to truth. <div eID="gen10145" type="x-p"/>
entries.a80cc084ff498e28dbd6f9b96034b4db9d44ab97: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6626"/><div sID="gen10146" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6626"/>3-5. The attending illustrations of God's awful justice on enemies (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.14">Psa 83:14</reference>) are seen in the disclosures of His almighty power on the elements of nature (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.46.2">Psa 46:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.77.17">77:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.6">Ha 3:6</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen10146" type="x-p"/>
entries.26b441e79fee88a255873d212e72a84563f71a27: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6627"/><div sID="gen10147" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6627"/><hi type="bold">6. heavens--</hi>or, their inhabitants (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.6">Psa 50:6</reference>), as opposed to "nations" in the latter clause (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.40.5">Is 40:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.18">66:18</reference>). <div eID="gen10147" type="x-p"/>
entries.022b97683288e7a5c06eea10fbb842e4da83f14e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6628"/><div sID="gen10148" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6628"/>7. Idolaters are utterly put to shame, for if angels must worship Him, how much more those who worshipped them.<div eID="gen10148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10149" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all ye gods--</hi>literally, "all ye angels" (<reference osisRef="Ps.8.5">Psa 8:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.138.1">138:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.6">He 1:6</reference>; 2:7). Paul quotes, not as a prophecy, but as language used in regard to the Lord Jehovah, who in the Old Testament theophania is the second person of the Godhead. <div eID="gen10149" type="x-p"/>
entries.be68d88a7f8100254b1f1389b5aa8732503496a2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6629"/><div sID="gen10150" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6629"/>8-9. The exaltation of Zion's king is joy to the righteous and sorrow to the wicked.<div eID="gen10150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10151" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">daughters of Judah--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.48.11">Psa 48:11</reference>). <div eID="gen10151" type="x-p"/>
entries.c3b8478c37c19017ea06d53247bd3b5497f2ceda: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6631"/><div sID="gen10153" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6631"/>10-12. Let gratitude for the blessings of providence and grace incite saints (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.3">Psa 4:3</reference>) to holy living. Spiritual blessings are in store, represented by light (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.1">Psa 27:1</reference>) and gladness. <div eID="gen10153" type="x-p"/>

entries.6d32bc8fbb9a1ad3907a0a0317d75eb5fb656f00: <div eID="gen21825" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21826" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21827" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21827" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21826" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21828" type="x-p"/> The reign of Jehovah, its nature and blessedness, <reference osisRef="Psa.97.1">Psa 97:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.97.2">Psa 97:2</reference>. He is fearful to the wicked, <reference osisRef="Psa.97.3-Psa.97.6">Psa 97:3-6</reference>. Idolaters shall be destroyed, <reference osisRef="Psa.97.7">Psa 97:7</reference>. The blessedness of the righteous, <reference osisRef="Psa.97.8-Psa.97.12">Psa 97:8-12</reference>. <div eID="gen21828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21829" type="x-p"/> This Psalm has no title either in the Hebrew or Chaldee; and in fourteen of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. it is written as a part of the preceding. In the Vulgate it is thus entitled, Psalmus David, quando terra ejus restituta est. "A Psalm of David when his land was restored;" the meaning of which I suppose to be, after he had obtained possession of the kingdom of Israel and Judah, and became king over all the tribes; or perhaps, after he had gained possession of all those countries which were originally granted to the Israelites in the Divine promise. See <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.1">1Chr 18:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.2">1Chr 18:2</reference>. The Septuagint is nearly to the same purpose, ὁτι ἡ γη αυτου καθισταται, "when his land was established:" so the Ethiopic and Arabic. The Syriac has, "A Psalm of David, in which he predicts the advent of Christ, (i.e., in the flesh), and through it his last appearing, (i.e., to judgment.") The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews <reference osisRef="1Chr.1.6">1Chr 1:6</reference>, quotes a part of the seventh verse of this Psalm, and applies it to Christ. Who the author was is uncertain: it is much in the spirit of David's finest compositions; and yet many learned men suppose it was written to celebrate the Lord's power and goodness in the restoration of the Jews from the Babylonish captivity. <div eID="gen21829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21830" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21831" type="x-p"/> The Lord reigneth - Here is a simple proposition, which is a self-evident axiom, and requires no proof: Jehovah is infinite and eternal; is possessed of unlimited power and unerring wisdom; as he is the Maker, so he must be the Governor, of all things. His authority is absolute, and his government therefore universal. In all places, on all occasions, and in all times, Jehovah reigns. <div eID="gen21831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21832" type="x-p"/> But this supreme King is not only called hwhy Yehovah, which signifies his infinite and eternal being, unlimited power, and unerring wisdom; and, as Creator, his universal government; but he is also ynd) Adonai, the Director and Judge. He directs human actions by his word, Spirit, and Providence. Hence are his laws and revelation in general; for the governed should know their governor, and should be acquainted with his laws, and the reasons on which obedience is founded. As Adonai or Director, he shows them the difference between good and evil; and their duty to their God, their neighbors, and themselves: and he finally becomes the Judge of their actions. But as his law is holy, and his commandment holy, just, and good, and man is in a fallen, sinful state; hence he reveals himself as; אלהים Elohim, God, entering into a gracious covenant with mankind, to enlighten his darkness, and help his infirmities; that he may see what is just, and be able to do it. But as this will not cancel the sins already committed, hence the necessity of a Savior, an atonement; and hence the incarnation, passion, death, and resurrection of our Lord Jesus. This is the provision made by the great God for the more effectual administration of his kingdom upon earth. Jehovah, Adonai, Elohim reigneth; et his animadversis, and these points considered, it is no wonder that the psalmist should add, <div eID="gen21832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21833" type="x-p"/> Let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad - The earth, the terraqueous globe; especially, here, the vast continents, over every part of which God's dominion extends. But it is not confined to them; it takes in the islands of the sea; all the multitude of those islands, even to the smallest inhabited rock; which are as much the objects of his care, the number of their inhabitants considered, as the vastest continents on which are founded the mightiest empires. All this government springs from his holiness, righteousness, and benignity; and is exercised in what we call providence, from pro, for, before, and video, to see, which word is well defined and applied by Cicero: Providentia est, per quam futurism aliquid videtur, antequam factum sit. "Providence is that by which any thing future is seen before it takes place." De Invent. c. 53. And, in reference to a Divine providence, he took up the general opinion, viz., Esse deos, et eorum providentia mundum administrari. De Divinat. c. 51, ad finem. "There are gods; and by their providence the affairs of the world are administered." <div eID="gen21833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21834" type="x-p"/> This providence is not only general, taking in the earth and its inhabitants, en masse; giving and establishing laws by which all things shall be governed; but it is also particular; it takes in the multitudes of the isles, as well as the vast continents; the different species as well as the genera; the individual, as well as the family. As every whole is composed of its parts, without the smallest of which it could not be a whole; so all generals are composed of particulars. And by the particular providence of God, the general providence is formed; he takes care of each individual; and, consequently, he takes care of the whole. Therefore, on the particular providence of God, the general providence is built; and the general providence could not exist without the particular, any more than a whole could subsist independently of its parts. It is by this particular providence that God governs the multitude of the isles, notices the fall of a sparrow, bottles; the tears of the mourner, and numbers the hairs of his followers. Now, as God is an infinitely wise and good Being, and governs the world in wisdom and goodness, the earth may well rejoice and the multitude of the isles be glad.
entries.4c5c4b9fb794720478d3ad58f7ec359b5036fdeb: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21835" type="x-p"/> Clouds and darkness are round about him - It is granted that this is a subject which cannot be comprehended. And why? Because God is infinite; he acts from his own counsels, which are infinite; in reference to ends which are also infinite: therefore, the reasons of his government cannot be comprehended by the feeble, limited powers of man. There must be clouds and darkness - an impenetrable obscurity, round about him; and we can no more comprehend him in what is called aeternitas a parte ante - the eternity that passed before time commenced, than we can in the aeternitas a parte post - the eternity that is to come, when time shall be no more. Yet such a Being cannot but see all things clearly, and do all things well; therefore the psalmist properly asserts: - <div eID="gen21835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21836" type="x-p"/> Righteousness and judgment are the habitation of his throne - Righteousness, צדק tsedek, the principle that acts according to justice and equity; that gives to all their due, and ever holds in all things an even balance. And judgment, משפט mishpat, the principle that discerns, orders, directs, and determines every thing according to truth and justice: these form the habitation of his throne; that is, his government and management of the world are according to these; and though we cannot see the springs, the secret counsels, and the times, which this omniscient and almighty <div eID="gen21836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21837" type="x-p"/> Father must ever have in his own power, yet we may rest assured that all his administration is wise, just, holy, good, and kind. For, although his counsels be inscrutable, and the dispensations of his providence be sometimes apparently unequal, yet righteousness and judgment are the habitation of his throne. <div eID="gen21837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21838" type="x-p"/> In this most sublime description,the psalmist, by the figure termed prosopopoeia, or personification, gives vitality and thought to all the subjects he employs; here, the very throne of God is animated; righteousness and judgment are two intellectual beings who support it. The fire, the lightnings, the earth, the heavens themselves, are all intellectual beings, which either accompany, go before him, or proclaim his majesty.
entries.1d6c47b3de3c827a86eaa4b85916cc3e13d3e16f: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21839" type="x-p"/> A fire goeth before him - Literally, this and the following verse may refer to the electric fluid, or to manifestations of the Divine displeasure, in which, by means of ethereal fire, God consumed his enemies. But fire is generally represented as an accompaniment of the appearances of the Supreme Being. He appeared on Mount Sinai in the midst of fire, thunder, and lightninys, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.16-Exo.19.18">Exo 19:16-18</reference>. Daniel, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.9">Dan 7:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.10">Dan 7:10</reference>, represents the Sovereign Judge as being on a throne which was a fiery flame, and the wheels of his chariot like burning fire; and a fiery streamer issuing from it, and coming forth from before him. St. Paul tells us (<reference osisRef="2Thes.1.8">2Thes 1:8</reference>) that the Lord Jesus shall be revealed from heaven with his mighty angels, in faming fire; and St. Peter, (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.7">2Pet 3:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.10">2Pet 3:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.11">2Pet 3:11</reference>), that when the Lord shall come to judgment the heavens and the earth shall be destroyed by fire. the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, the elements melt with fervent heat, and the earth and its works be burnt up. Here then, will appear: - "Our God in grandeur, and our world on fire." <div eID="gen21839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21840" type="x-p"/> Burneth up his enemies round about - The fire is his pioneer which destroys all the hinderances in his way, and makes him a plain passage.
entries.963bae04543d77456a839c1c4aa6cba0a1038d61: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen21840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21841" type="x-p"/> His lightnings enlightened the world - Though this be no more than a majestic description of the coming of the Lord, to confound his enemies and succor his followers, yet some spiritualize the passage, and say, the lightnings signify the apostles, who enlightened the world by their heavenly doctrine. <div eID="gen21841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21842" type="x-p"/> The earth saw, and trembled - The earth is represented as a sentient being. It saw the terrible majesty of God; and trembled through terror, fearing it should be destroyed on account of the wickedness of its inhabitants.
entries.e3497d09402ebc1c2f9410d48db524422e47f603: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen21842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21843" type="x-p"/> The hills melted like wax - The fire of God seized on and liquefied them, so that they no longer opposed his march; and the mountains before him became a plain. <div eID="gen21843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21844" type="x-p"/> The Lord of the whole earth - אדון כל הארץ adon col haarets, the Director, Stay, and Support of the whole earth. The universal Governor, whose jurisdiction is not confined to any one place; but who, having created all, governs all that he has made.
entries.0f0c580fceba0d0cb3bbcb23d245daccfe9af8dc: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen21844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21845" type="x-p"/> The heavens declare his righteousness - They also, in this poetic description, become intelligent beings, and proclaim the majesty and the mercy of the Most High. Metaphorically, they may be said to declare his glory. Their magnitude, number, revolutions, order, influence, and harmony, proclaim the wondrous skill, matchless wisdom, and unlimited power of the Sovereign of the universe. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Psa.19.1-Psa.19.14">Psa 19:1-14</reference> (note). <div eID="gen21845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21846" type="x-p"/> And all the people see his glory - Whatsoever God has made proclaims his eternal power and Godhead; and who, from a contemplation of the work of his hands, can be ignorant of his being and providence?
entries.38c7e04a9dce92bc4cfc20b03d1c9339361d8642: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen21846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21847" type="x-p"/> Confounded be fell they - Rather, They shall be confounded that boast themselves in idols. There is a remarkable play on the letters here, המתהללים hammithhalelim, who move like madmen; referring to the violent gestures practiced in idolatrous rites. <div eID="gen21847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21848" type="x-p"/> Of idols - באלילים baelilim, in vanities, emptinesses; who "make much ado about nothing," and take a mad and painful pleasure in ridiculous and unprofitable ceremonies of religion. <div eID="gen21848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21849" type="x-p"/> Worship him - Who? Jesus: so says the apostle, <reference osisRef="Heb.1.6">Heb 1:6</reference>. Who will dare to dispute his authority? <div eID="gen21849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21850" type="x-p"/> All ye gods - Οἱ αγγελοι αυτου, his angels: so the Septuagint and the apostle: "Let all the angels of God worship him:" and the words are most certainly applied to the Savior of the world by the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews; see the note there. The Chaldee says: "All nations who worship idols shall adore him."
entries.554081424863847b41b81a9d2c5af632709fa5c4: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen21850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21851" type="x-p"/> Zion heard, and was glad - All the land of Israel, long desolated, heard of the judgments which God had shown among the enemies of his people. <div eID="gen21851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21852" type="x-p"/> And the daughters of Judah - All the villages of the land - Zion as the mother, and all the villages in the country as her daughters, rejoice in the deliverance of God's people.
entries.186771f8b9e07445a271662c7d39e9b74c67b258: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen21852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21853" type="x-p"/> For thou, Lord, art high - Thou art infinitely exalted above men and angels.
entries.ebad3f27b6a73df347641e867ad7688f3ab19154: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen21853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21854" type="x-p"/> Ye that love the Lord hate evil - Because it is inconsistent with his love to you, as well as your love to him. <div eID="gen21854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21855" type="x-p"/> He preserveth the souls of his saints - The saints, חסידיו chasidaiv, his merciful people: their souls - lives, are precious in his sight. He preserves them; keeps them from every evil, and every enemy. <div eID="gen21855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21856" type="x-p"/> Out of the hand of the wicked - From his power and influence.
entries.82055f5c9f41c97a12401447e02742d1b6578264: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen21856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21857" type="x-p"/> Light is sown for the righteous - The Divine light in the soul of man is a seed which takes root, and springs up and increases thirty, sixty, and a hundred fold. Gladness is also a seed: it is sown, and, if carefully improved and cultivated, will also multiply itself into thousands. Every grace of God is a seed which he intends should produce a thousand fold in the hearts of genuine believers. We do not so much require more grace from God, as the cultivation of what we have received. God will not give more, unless we improve what we have got. Remember the parable of the talents. Let the light and gladness be faithfully cultivated, and they will multiply themselves till the whole body shall be full of light, and the whole soul full of happiness. But it is the righteous only for whom the light is sown; and the upright in heart alone for whom the gladness is sown. <div eID="gen21857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21858" type="x-p"/> The words may also signify that, however distressed or persecuted the righteous and the upright may be, it shall not be always so. As surely as the grain that is sown in the earth shall vegetate, and bring forth its proper fruit in its season, so surely shall light - prosperity, and gladness - comfort and peace, be communicated to them. They also will spring up in due time.
entries.bf5076ca03156fb34aeb63210ba0ddcb8c45fe84: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen21858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21859" type="x-p"/> Rejoice in the Lord, ye righteous - It is your privilege to be happy. Exult in him through whom ye have received the atonement. Rejoice; but let it be in the Lord. All other joy is the mirth of fools, which is as the crackling of thorns under a pot - it is a luminous blaze for a moment, and leaves nothing but smoke and ashes behind. <div eID="gen21859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21860" type="x-p"/> At the remembrance of his holiness - But why should you give thanks at the remembrance that God is holy? Because he has said, Be ye holy; for I am holy: and in holiness alone true happiness is to be found. As he, therefore, who hath called you is holy; so be ye holy in all manner of conversation. False Christians hate the doctrine of Christian holiness; they are willing to be holy in another, but not holy in themselves. There is too much cross-bearing and self-denial in the doctrine of holiness for them. A perfect heart they neither expect nor wish. <div eID="gen21860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21861" type="x-p"/> The analysis considers the whole Psalm as relating to Jesus Christ and the last judgment: so it was understood by several of the ancient fathers. The reader may take it in either sense.  <chapter eID="Ps.97"/> <div eID="gen21861" type="x-p"/>

entries.0448c8dca4e9faac0a8171b87b63f1c0773aa0aa: <div eID="gen9950" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Breaking Through of the Kingdom of God, the Judge and Saviour</title> <div sID="gen9951" type="x-p"/> This Psalm, too, has the coming of Jahve, who enters upon His kingdom through judgment, as its theme, and the watchword “Jahve is King” as its key-note. The lxx inscribes it: τῷ Δαυίδ ὅτε ἡ γῆ αὐτοῦ καθίσταται (καθίστατο); Jerome: <hi type="italic">quando terra ejus restituta est</hi>. The τῷ Δαυίδ is worthless; the time of restoration, from which it takes its rise, is the post-exilic, for it is composed, as mosaic-work, out of the earlier original passages of Davidic and Asaphic Psalms and of the prophets, more especially of Isaiah, and is entirely an expression of the religious consciousness which resulted from the Exile.
entries.8731e9d156a30934aa48d0a2ac3b523a59f2bfcb: <reference osisRef="Ps.97.1-Ps.97.3">Psa 97:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen9951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9952" type="x-p"/> We have here nothing but echoes of the older literature: <reference osisRef="Ps.97.1">Psa 97:1</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.42.10-Isa.42.12">Isa 42:10-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.5">Isa 51:5</reference>; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.97.2">Psa 97:2</reference></hi>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.18.10">Psa 18:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.12">Psa 18:12</reference>; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.97.2">Psa 97:2</reference></hi> = <reference osisRef="Ps.89.15">Psa 89:15</reference>; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.97.3">Psa 97:3</reference></hi>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.50.3">Psa 50:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.9">Psa 18:9</reference>; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.97.3">Psa 97:3</reference></hi>, cf. Isa 42:25. Beginning with the visible coming of the kingdom of God in the present, with מלך ה the poet takes his stand upon the standpoint of the kingdom which is come. With it also comes rich material for universal joy. תּגל is indicative, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.96.11">Psa 96:11</reference> and frequently. רבּים are all, for all of them are in fact many (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.52.15">Isa 52:15</reference>). The description of the theophany, for which the way is preparing in <reference osisRef="Ps.97.2">Psa 97:2</reference>, also reminds one of Hab. 3. God’s enshrouding Himself in darkness bears witness to His judicial earnestness. Because He comes as Judge, the basis of His royal throne and of His judgment-seat is also called to mind. His harbinger is fire, which consumes His adversaries on every side, as that which broke forth out of the pillar of cloud once consumed the Egyptians.
entries.b6c505ac60db3b6624adb1b8d4a19d112dd3efa2: <reference osisRef="Ps.97.4-Ps.97.6">Psa 97:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen9952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9953" type="x-p"/> Again we have nothing but echoes of the older literature: <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.97.4">Psa 97:4</reference></hi> = <reference osisRef="Ps.77.19">Psa 77:19</reference>; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.97.4">Psa 97:4</reference></hi>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.77.17">Psa 77:17</reference>; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.97.5">Psa 97:5</reference></hi>, cf. Mic 1:4; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.97.5">Psa 97:5</reference></hi>, cf. Mic 4:13; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.97.6">Psa 97:6</reference></hi> = <reference osisRef="Ps.50.6">Psa 50:6</reference>; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.97.6">Psa 97:6</reference></hi>, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.35.2">Isa 35:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.5">Isa 40:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.10">Isa 52:10</reference>; Isa 66:18. The poet goes on to describe that which is future with historical certainty. That which <reference osisRef="Ps.77.19">Psa 77:19</reference> says of the manifestation of God in the earlier times he transfers to the revelation of God in the last time. The earth sees it, and begins to tremble in consequence of it. The reading ותּחל, according to Hitzig (cf. Ew. §232, <hi type="italic">b</hi>) traditional, is, however, only an error of pointing that has been propagated; the correct reading is the reading of Heidenheim and Baer, restored according to MSS, ותּחל (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.3">1Sa 31:3</reference>), like ותּבן, ותּקם, ותּרם, and ותּשׂם. The figure of the wax is found even in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.3">Psa 68:3</reference>; and Jahve is also called “Lord of the whole earth” in Zec 4:14; Zec 6:5. The proclamation of the heavens is an expression of joy, Psa 96:11. They proclaim the judicial strictness with which Jahve, in accordance with His promises, carries out His plan of salvation, the realization of which has reached its goal in the fact that all men see the glory of God.
entries.e07e2646009ae83489ed0e2c91e5adbb971434fc: <reference osisRef="Ps.97.7-Ps.97.8">Psa 97:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen9953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9954" type="x-p"/> When the glory of Jahve becomes manifest, everything that is opposed to it will be punished and consumed by its light. Those who serve idols will become conscious of their delusion with shame and terror, <reference osisRef="Isa.42.17">Isa 42:17</reference>; Jer 10:14. The superhuman powers (lxx ἄγγελοι), deified by the heathen, then bow down to Him who alone is <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> in absolute personality. השׁתּחווּ is not imperative (lxx, Syriac), for as a command this clause would be abrupt and inconsequential, but the perfect of that which actually takes place. The quotation in <reference osisRef="Heb.1.6">Heb 1:6</reference> is taken from <reference osisRef="Deut.32.43">Deu 32:43</reference>, lxx. In <reference osisRef="Ps.97.8">Psa 97:8</reference> (after <reference osisRef="Ps.48.12">Psa 48:12</reference>) the survey of the poet again comes back to his own nation. When Zion hears that Jahve has appeared, and all the world and all the powers bow down to Him, she rejoices; for it is in fact her God whose kingship has come to the acknowledge. And all the daughter-churches of the Jewish land exult together with the mother-church over the salvation which dawns through judgments.
entries.0d00cf9775f26e0aae64d32c5d42e1fb00b493d6: <reference osisRef="Ps.97.9">Psa 97:9</reference> <div eID="gen9954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9955" type="x-p"/> This distichic epiphonema (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.97.9">Psa 97:9</reference></hi> = Ps 83:19; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.97.9">Psa 97:9</reference></hi>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.47.3">Psa 47:3</reference>, 10) might close the Psalm; there follows still, however, a hortatory strophe (which was perhaps not added till later on).
entries.0d793ea4f5a2cc12593f8293a0d08a2476739820: <reference osisRef="Ps.97.10-Ps.97.12">Psa 97:10-12</reference> <div eID="gen9955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9956" type="x-p"/> It is true <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.97.12">Psa 97:12</reference></hi> is = <reference osisRef="Ps.32.11">Psa 32:11</reference>, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.97.12">Psa 97:12</reference></hi> = <reference osisRef="Ps.30.5">Psa 30:5</reference>, and the promise in <reference osisRef="Ps.97.10">Psa 97:10</reference> is the same as in <reference osisRef="Ps.37.28">Psa 37:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.34.21">Psa 34:21</reference>; but as to the rest, particularly <reference osisRef="Ps.97.11">Psa 97:11</reference>, this strophe is original. It is an encouraging admonition to fidelity in an age in which an effeminate spirit of looking longingly towards lit. ogling heathenism was rife, and stedfast adherence to Jahve was threatened with loss of life. Those who are faithful in their confession, as in the Maccabaean age (Ἀσιδαῖοι), are called חסדיו. The beautiful figure in <reference osisRef="Ps.97.11">Psa 97:11</reference> is misapprehended by the ancient versions, inasmuch as they read זרח (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.4">Psa 112:4</reference>) instead of זרע. זרע does not here signify sown = strewn into the earth, but strewn along his life’s way, so that he, the righteous one, advances step by step in the light. Hitzig rightly compares ki'dnatai ski'dnatai, used of the dawn and of the sun. Of the former Virgil also says, <hi type="italic">Et jam prima novo spargebat lumine terras</hi>.  <chapter eID="Ps.97"/> <div eID="gen9956" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 97
The description which we have of the kingdom of God in this psalm, does not apply to the state of it under the Law. We may infer, accordingly, that it contains a prediction of that kingdom of Christ, which was erected upon the introduction of the Gospel. The Psalmist, while he commends it to us by insisting upon its greatness and glory, so well calculated to compel the reverential fear of men, gives an amiable representation of it, by informing us that it has been erected for the salvation of mankind sinners.
Psalm 97:1-5
1. Jehovah reigns: let the earth rejoice, let the great islands
“Ou, que beaucoup d’isles.” — Fr marg “Or, let the many isles.” Horsley and some other critics object to translating the original word, איים, iyim, by isles He reads, “Let the various settlements of man rejoice:” on which he observes, “I cannot more exactly render the force of the Hebrew איים, than by this periphrasis. The English language hath no single word to convey the same idea; and the word ‘isles’ or ‘islands,’ hath hardly any relation to it.” Fry’s note here is as follows: — “The Hebrew terms rendered, ‘the multitude of the isles,’ ‘the various settlements of men,’ ‘the extended shores,’ seem in a special manner to designate these western parts of the world, which were known as distant coasts visited by the ships of Tyre. All Europe might originally fall under this denomination, with some parts of the sea coasts of Africa, and even of Asia; nor can there be any doubt, that all subsequent discoveries by sea, once uninhabited, but now colonized, and settled from the old countries, would be designated by this term. Some nations of this description are called upon, in particular, to rejoice in the Savior’s appearing.”
be glad. 2. Clouds and darkness are round about him; righteousness and judgment are the habitation
The word מכון, mechon, here rendered “habitation,” is from כון, kun, he prepared, fitted, confirmed “It is used,” says Hammond, “for a place, seat, but especially a basis, whereon anything is set: from whence the LXX. had their μεχωςὼθ, (the very Hebrew מכונות) for basis, 1 Kings 7:27. The Chaldee here retains the original מכון, but the LXX., from the notion of the verb for fitting, read κατόρθωσις, ‘the setting right of his throne;’ the Syriac, by way of paraphrase, ‘by equity and judgment thy throne is confirmed:’ all which concur to the notion of basis or foundation, which is the thing that gives the rectitude first, and then the stability, to the chair or throne that is set on it. And so that is unquestionably the right, intelligible rendering of the phrase, ‘Righteousness and judgment are the (not habitation but) basis of his throne,’ i e., his sentences, decrees, judicatures, are all built upon righteousness and judgment, as a throne is built and established on a foundation.”
of his throne. 3. A fire shall go before his face, and shall burn up his enemies round about. 4. His lightnings enlightened the world; the earth shall see, and tremble. 5. The hills flow down like wax at the presence of Jehovah, at the presence of the Lord of the whole earth.
 
1 Jehovah reigns His inviting men to rejoice, is a proof that the reign of God is inseparably connected with the salvation and best happiness of mankind. And, the joy he speaks of being common to the whole world and to the regions beyond the seas, it is evident that he predicts the enlargement of God’s kingdom, which had been confined within the narrow boundaries of Judea, to a far wider extent. The Psalmist, in setting forth the various particulars of the Divine glory in the four verses which follow, would seek to impress all men with a reverential fear of him. Thus he gives us a representation of the formidable majesty attaching to God, that he may dash and humble vain confidence and carnal pride. A cloudy sky overawes us more than a clear one, as the darkness produces a peculiar effect upon the senses. The Psalmist makes use of this symbol, no doubt, to impress the world with the greater reverence of God. Others refine more upon the words, and think that clouds are said to be round about God, to check human rashness and presumption, and restrain that excessive curiosity which would pry more than is fit into the mysteries of Godhead. This is an interpretation of the words which makes them convey a very useful lesson; but I am against all refined renderings, and think that the Psalmist intended in associating darkness with God, to impress the hearts of men with a fear of him in general.
“Que le Prophete a voulu par ce regard obscur de Dieu, toucher au vif les coeurs des hommes, afin qu’ils tremblent.” — Fr.
The same meaning is brought out in the remaining context, when fire is said to go before him, and burn up his enemies, his lightnings to shake the earth, and the mountains to flow down. Should any object that this does not agree with what was said of the joy which his kingdom diffuses, I might answer, first, that although God is ready on his part to diffuse blessedness wherever he reigns, all are not capable of appreciating it. Besides, as I have already hinted, the truth is one of use to believers, humbling the pride of the flesh, and deepening their adoration of God. God’s throne is represented as founded in justice and judgment, to denote the benefit which we derive from it. The greatest misery which can be conceived of, is that of living without righteousness and judgment, and the Psalmist mentions it as matter of praise exclusively due to God, that when he reigns, righteousness revives in the world. He as evidently denies that we can have any righteousness, till God subjects us to the yoke of his word, by the gentle but powerful influences of his Spirit. A great proportion of men obstinately resist and reject the government of God. Hence the Psalmist was forced to exhibit God in his severer aspect, to teach the wicked that their perverse opposition will not pass unpunished. When God draws near to men in mercy, and they fail to welcome him with becoming reverence and respect, this implies impiety of a very aggravated description; on which account it is that the language of denunciation suits with the kingdom of Christ. The Psalmist intimates that those who should despise God in the person of his only-begotten Son, will feel in due time and certainly the awful weight of his majesty. So much is implied in the expression used — The earth Shall See. For the wicked, when they find that their attempts are vain in fighting against God, resort to subterfuge and concealment. The Psalmist declares that they would not succeed by any such vain artifice in hiding themselves from God.
Psalm 97:6-8
6. The heavens have declared his righteousness, and all the people have seen his glory. 7. Confounded be all those who serve graven images, who glory in their inventions;
“Ou, idoles.” Fr marg “Or, idols.” The original word here is אלילים elilim See note 2, page 50.
let all the gods worship before him. 8. Zion heard, and was glad; and the daughters of Judah
“Judah’s daughters, the inferior towns and villages of Judea, so called with reference to the metropolis, or mother city. This is a very elegant kind of personification, by which the subject, adjunct, accident, effect, or the like, of any thing or place is called the son, or, as in this instance, the daughter of that thing or place. Hence the Hebrew poets often introduce, as it were, on the stage, nations, countries, or kingdoms, clothed in the dress of women, and performing all the functions suited to such a character. The practice is familiar to our minds; but probably it is so rendered by our habitual acquaintance with the Hebrew idiom, to which it appears to owe its origin.” — Mant on Psalms 48:11.
rejoiced because of thy judgments, O Jehovah!
